title: Are US Long Bonds A Buy? (Part II)
gist: The US Treasury under Scott Bessent is attempting a "Treasury twist" — buying back long-dated debt while issuing more at the short end — to suppress long-term yields and flatten the curve, but the Federal Reserve under chair Kevin Warsh is simultaneously untwisting its balance sheet away from long-term securities, releasing duration back to the market. The unresolved question is which side moves faster, with the Treasury's first expanded buyback on September 9 as the immediate test.

insights.claim: The US Treasury plans to buy back more debt at the long end of the curve while issuing more at the short end, a maturity-mix shift described as a "Treasury twist".
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Debt-management policy, not just Fed policy, is now an active lever on the long end — issuance composition becomes a tradable macro variable.

insights.claim: Numerous forces are working to push US long-end yields higher, so the Treasury secretary faces an uphill task in suppressing long-term yields through buybacks alone.

insights.so_what: Tempers the consensus that official buybacks automatically cap long yields — sizing a long-duration position on the twist alone carries asymmetric risk.

insights.so_what: Fed balance-sheet composition is a direct offset to Treasury buybacks; net duration supply, not gross buyback size, is the number that matters for long yields.
